title: Zhou, Spring and Autumn and the Hundred Schools
bigQuestion: Why did an age of war and disorder produce so many great thinkers?

story.title: The Adviser on the Road
story.kicker: A teacher travels from court to court with his students, and no ruler will put his ideas to work.
paragraphs: The ox cart bumps along a dirt road. Inside sits a man in his fifties, with a handful of students walking beside him. He has left his home state of Lu. He is looking for a ruler who will listen. His name is Kong Qiu. Later ages will call him Kongzi, or Confucius.

At each court the pattern is the same. A duke greets him politely and asks for advice. Confucius talks about ruling by good example, about ritual and about caring for the people. The duke nods. Then he asks how to win his next war. Confucius has little to say about armies, and he soon moves on.

Some days go badly. Tradition tells that the group once ran out of food between two states, and some students grew angry. "Does a gentleman also face such hardship?" one asks. Confucius answers that a gentleman stays steady in hard times, while a small person loses control.

After about fourteen years on the road, Confucius returns home. He never gains the high office he hoped for. He spends his last years teaching. Yet his students will carry his words across China, and a book of his sayings, the Analects, will be read for over two thousand years.
story.think: Why might a teacher keep traveling and giving advice when no ruler takes it?

lessons.title: The Zhou Take Power
lessons.mainIdea: The Zhou dynasty overthrew the Shang and explained its rule with the idea of the Mandate of Heaven.
reading: Around 1046 BCE (traditional dates run earlier, to 1122 BCE), the Zhou people defeated the Shang kings at the Battle of Muye. The Zhou founded a *dynasty*, a line of rulers from one family. It lasted until 256 BCE, longer than any other in Chinese history.

The Zhou needed to explain why they had the right to rule. Their answer appears in the Book of Documents, one of the oldest Chinese texts. It says that Heaven (*tian*) gives the right to rule to a virtuous family. When a ruler becomes cruel and careless, Heaven takes that right away and gives it to another.

This idea is called the *Mandate of Heaven*. The Zhou said the last Shang king had been cruel, so Heaven had passed the mandate to them. Later Chinese dynasties used the same idea for about three thousand years, both to claim power and to judge rulers who failed.

words.d: a line of rulers from the same family who rule one after another
the idea that Heaven gives the right to rule to a virtuous ruler and can take it away
Heaven; in early Chinese texts, the high power that watches over rulers and the world

look.cite: Standard dates, e.g. The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the Zhou conquest and the end of the Zhou dynasty?

check.q: What does the Mandate of Heaven explain?
choices: Why a ruler has the right to rule and can lose it
check.why: The Mandate of Heaven says Heaven grants rule to virtuous rulers and removes it from cruel ones.

check.q: Which dynasty did the Zhou overthrow?
check.why: The Zhou defeated the Shang, c. 1046 BCE.

check.q: In which old text does the Mandate of Heaven appear?
check.why: Speeches in the Book of Documents explain the Zhou claim to Heaven's mandate.

lessons.title: The Duke of Zhou
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius admired the early Zhou, especially the Duke of Zhou, as a model of good government and ritual.
reading: After the Zhou conquest, the young king was too young to rule alone. His uncle, the *Duke of Zhou*, ruled for him. Tradition says the duke then handed power back when the king came of age. Tradition also credits him with setting the rules of court ritual and music.

Five centuries later, Confucius looked back at the early Zhou as a golden age. In Analects 7.5 he sighs that he has not dreamed of the Duke of Zhou for a long time, a sign to him that he was growing old. In Analects 3.14 he says the Zhou learned from the two dynasties before it, and so he follows the Zhou.

Historians note that much of this picture is idealized. The early Zhou fought wars and put down revolts. But for Confucius and his followers, the early Zhou stood for *ritual* order and rulers who led by virtue. That ideal shaped Confucian thinking.

words.d: an early Zhou leader who ruled for a young king; Confucius admired him as a model
a set of formal actions done in a set way, such as ceremonies, greetings and offerings
shown as better or more perfect than it really was

look.title: Following the Zhou
look.text: Chau had the advantage of viewing the two past dynasties. How complete and elegant are its regulations! I follow Chau.
look.cite: Confucius, Analects 3.14, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (2nd ed., 1893)
look.prompt: Why does Confucius say he follows the Zhou (Legge spells it Chau)?

check.q: Why did the Duke of Zhou rule for a time?
choices: The young king was too young to rule alone
check.why: Tradition says the Duke of Zhou ruled for his young nephew and then returned power.

check.q: In Analects 3.14, which dynasty does Confucius say he follows?
check.why: Confucius says the Zhou learned from the two earlier dynasties, so he follows the Zhou.

check.q: What do historians say about Confucius's picture of the early Zhou?
check.why: Historians note the early Zhou also had wars and revolts; Confucius's picture is an ideal.

lessons.title: A Kingdom Breaks Apart
lessons.mainIdea: After 771 BCE the Zhou kings lost real power, and many states competed and fought through the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods.
reading: In 771 BCE, invaders and rebels killed a Zhou king, and the court fled east to Luoyang. From then on, Zhou kings kept their title and rituals but had little real power. Local lords ruled their own states and fought one another.

Historians divide the next centuries into two parts. The *Spring and Autumn period* (771–476 BCE) is named after a history of the state of Lu, the Spring and Autumn Annals. The *Warring States period* (475–221 BCE) is named for its constant wars among seven large states.

Over time, small states were swallowed by larger ones. Armies grew to hundreds of thousands of soldiers. Rulers needed clever advisers to plan wars, collect taxes and run their lands. That need opened the door for a new kind of person: the traveling thinker.

words.d: 771–476 BCE, when the Zhou kings were weak and many states competed
475–221 BCE, when seven large states fought until Qin united China
here, a territory ruled by its own lord or king, like Lu, Qi or Qin

look.title: Weak King, Strong Lords
look.text: Picture a school where the principal still gives speeches and hands out awards, but no one follows the rules. Each grade makes its own laws. The biggest grades take over the smaller ones' rooms.
look.prompt: How is this like the Zhou after 771 BCE? Where does the comparison not fit?

check.q: What happened to Zhou kings after 771 BCE?
choices: They kept their title but lost real power
check.why: After the move east, Zhou kings kept rituals but local lords held real power.

check.q: Where does the name Spring and Autumn come from?
choices: A history of Lu, the Spring and Autumn Annals
check.why: The period is named for the Spring and Autumn Annals, a history of the state of Lu.

check.q: Which dates belong to the Warring States period?
check.why: The Warring States period runs from 475 to 221 BCE, when Qin unified China.

lessons.title: A Teacher from Lu
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius (traditional dates 551–479 BCE) was a teacher from the state of Lu who hoped to restore good order through virtue and ritual.
reading: Tradition dates Confucius's life to 551–479 BCE. He was born in the state of Lu, in what is now Shandong province. His family name was Kong and his given name Qiu. The title *Kongzi* means Master Kong; Jesuit writers in the 1600s turned the longer form Kong Fuzi into the Latin Confucius.

According to later accounts, Confucius grew up poor and worked in small jobs, such as keeping granaries. He loved learning. The Analects reports him saying that at fifteen he set his heart on learning (2.4). He held some office in Lu, though scholars debate how high.

Confucius became famous as a teacher. Tradition says he taught students from rich and poor families alike. In Analects 7.7 he says he never refused to teach anyone who brought even a small gift. His students later spread his teachings and served in governments.

words.d: Master Kong, the Chinese title of Confucius
beliefs and stories passed down over time; traditional dates are those accepted by long custom
the collection of sayings of Confucius and his students, in 20 books

look.title: A Life in Stages
look.text: At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts.
look.cite: Confucius, Analects 2.4, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (2nd ed., 1893)
look.prompt: What does Confucius say changed in him at each age? Why might a teacher describe his own growth?

check.q: What are Confucius's traditional dates?
check.why: Tradition dates Confucius's life to 551–479 BCE.

check.q: Where did the name Confucius come from?
check.why: Jesuit missionaries in the 1600s turned Kong Fuzi into the Latin form Confucius.

check.q: What did Confucius say in Analects 7.7?
choices: He never refused a student who brought a small gift
check.why: In 7.7 Confucius says he never refused instruction to anyone who came with even a small gift.

lessons.title: Looking for a Ruler
lessons.mainIdea: Like many thinkers of his time, Confucius traveled from state to state looking for a ruler who would put his ideas into practice.
reading: Around 497 BCE, according to Sima Qian's account, Confucius left Lu. For about fourteen years he traveled through states such as Wei, Chen and Cai. He met rulers and gave advice, but none gave him the power to reform their government.

The Analects records people who doubted him. In 14.38 (numbered 14.41 in Legge), a gatekeeper describes Confucius as the man who knows a thing cannot be done and still keeps doing it. In book 18, hermits tell his students that the world is a flood no one can stop, so why try.

Confucius was not alone. In the Warring States period many *advisers* moved from court to court. Rulers welcomed them because they wanted ideas that would make their states strong. Advisers hoped to find a ruler who would listen.

words.d: a person who gives advice to a ruler about how to govern
a person who lives apart from society, often for spiritual or moral reasons

look.title: The Gatekeeper's Words
look.text: A gatekeeper asks a student of Confucius where he comes from. When he hears the answer, he says: Is he not the one who knows it cannot be done, and keeps on doing it?
look.cite: Analects 14.38 (14.41 in Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 1893), paraphrased
look.prompt: Is the gatekeeper praising or mocking Confucius? How could a reader argue each side?

check.q: Why did Confucius travel for about fourteen years?
choices: To find a ruler who would use his ideas
check.why: Confucius traveled among states seeking a ruler who would put his teachings into practice.

check.q: Who says Confucius knows a thing cannot be done yet keeps doing it?
check.why: In Analects 14.38 (14.41 in Legge), a gatekeeper describes Confucius this way.

check.q: Why did rulers welcome traveling advisers?
choices: They wanted ideas to make their states strong
check.why: In a time of competition and war, rulers sought advice that would strengthen their states.

lessons.title: Legends and Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Historians separate what early sources show about Confucius from later legends that grew around him.
reading: Much of what people know about Confucius comes from two sources. One is the Analects, compiled by his students and their students over many years. The other is a biography in the Records of the Historian (*Shiji*) by Sima Qian, finished around 94 BCE, about four centuries after Confucius died.

A *primary source* is evidence from the time being studied. For Confucius, even the Analects was collected after his death, and scholars debate which parts are oldest. Sima Qian used older records, but he also included stories that historians cannot check.

Later ages added *legends*: that a unicorn-like qilin appeared at his birth, or that he edited all of the Five Classics. Legends matter because they show how people honored him. Historians simply label them as legend, not as proven fact.

words.d: evidence from the time being studied, such as a letter, inscription or record
Records of the Historian, a history of China by Sima Qian, finished c. 94 BCE
a story passed down about a person or event that cannot be proven

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: Claim A: Confucius came from the state of Lu. Claim B: A qilin appeared when he was born. Claim C: His sayings were collected by students after his death. Claim D: He personally edited every one of the Five Classics.
look.prompt: Which claims are well supported by early sources, and which are later traditions? Explain how you decided.

check.q: Who wrote the Shiji, with its biography of Confucius?
check.why: Sima Qian finished the Records of the Historian around 94 BCE.

check.q: What is a primary source?
choices: Evidence from the time being studied
check.why: A primary source comes from the time being studied.

check.q: How do historians treat stories like the qilin at Confucius's birth?
choices: As legend that shows how people honored him
check.why: Historians label such stories as legend and study them for what they show about later honor.

lessons.title: Why Chaos Made Thinkers
lessons.mainIdea: War, change and competition among states led many thinkers to ask how people and states should be ordered.
reading: Why did so many philosophers appear in the Warring States period? Historians point to several causes. The old order of the Zhou had broken down, so people asked what should replace it. Rulers paid for good ideas. And writing spread beyond a small group of court officials.

The state of Qi even founded a center of learning, the *Jixia Academy*, around the 300s BCE. Scholars from many schools lived there on state support and debated. Mencius and Xunzi are both linked to Qi in the sources.

Thinkers argued about the same basic questions. How should a ruler govern? Is human nature good or bad? Should people follow ritual, law, love for all, or the natural Way? Their answers became the *Hundred Schools of Thought*. "Hundred" means many, not exactly one hundred.

words.d: the many schools of philosophy in China c. 500–221 BCE; hundred means many
a center of learning in the state of Qi where thinkers of many schools debated
the study of basic questions about how to live, know and govern

look.title: One Question, Many Answers
look.text: A ruler asks: "My state is in danger. What should I do?" Adviser 1: "Lead by good example and keep the rites." Adviser 2: "Write strict laws and punish anyone who breaks them." Adviser 3: "Stop fighting, and care for all people equally." Adviser 4: "Do less. Stop forcing things."
look.prompt: Which answer sounds most like each school you will meet in this section? What does each assume about people?

check.q: What does 'hundred' mean in Hundred Schools of Thought?
check.why: The phrase means many schools, not a precise count.

check.q: What was the Jixia Academy?
choices: A center of learning in Qi
check.why: The Jixia Academy in Qi supported scholars from many schools who debated there.

check.q: Which is one reason historians give for the rise of the Hundred Schools?
choices: The Zhou order had broken down, and rulers wanted new ideas
China was at peace for centuries
check.why: The collapse of Zhou order and competition among states created demand for new ideas.

lessons.title: Confucians and Daoists
lessons.mainIdea: Confucians taught virtue, ritual and learning, while Daoists taught following the natural Way and acting without forcing.
reading: The *Confucians* (in Chinese, the Ru, or scholars) followed Confucius. They taught that society becomes orderly when people practice *ren*, humane care for others, and *li*, ritual and proper conduct. Rulers, they said, should lead by moral example, and people should keep learning all their lives.

The *Daoists* are named for the *Dao*, the Way. The Daodejing, a short poetic book linked to Laozi, says the Dao cannot be fully put into words. It praises *wu wei*, often translated as "non-action" or acting without forcing. The Zhuangzi adds funny stories and puzzles.

The two schools disagreed. The Daodejing, ch. 18, suggests that talk of humaneness and rightness appears only after the great Way is lost. Confucians answered that people need learning and ritual to grow. Yet many Chinese readers later drew on both.

words.d: humaneness; caring for others; the highest virtue in Confucius's teaching
ritual and proper conduct, from ceremonies to everyday manners
the Way; in the Daodejing, the source and pattern of all things
acting without forcing, sometimes translated as non-action; a key Daoist idea

look.title: When the Great Way Is Lost
look.text: When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed, benevolence and righteousness came into vogue.
look.cite: Daodejing ch. 18, trans. James Legge, The Tao Teh King, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
look.prompt: What is the Daodejing suggesting about Confucian virtues here? How might a Confucian reply?

check.q: Which term means humane care for others in Confucius's teaching?
check.why: Ren is humaneness, the central Confucian virtue.

check.q: What does wu wei mean?
check.why: Wu wei, a Daoist idea, means acting without forcing, or non-action.

check.q: What does Daodejing ch. 18 suggest?
choices: Ritual is the source of the Way
Talk of benevolence appears after the Way is lost
check.why: Chapter 18 says benevolence and righteousness came into vogue when the great Way was no longer followed.

lessons.title: Mohists and Legalists
lessons.mainIdea: Mohists taught care for all and opposed aggressive war; Legalists taught strict laws, rewards and punishments.
reading: The *Mohists* followed Mozi (c. 470–391 BCE). He taught *jian ai*, often translated "universal love" or impartial care: caring for other people's families and states as for your own. Mohists opposed attacking wars and spending too much on funerals and music.

The *Legalists* took a very different view. Thinkers like Shang Yang and Han Feizi argued that people act mainly for reward and to avoid punishment. So a ruler should make clear laws, enforce them strictly, and reward farming and fighting. The state of Qin used these ideas and grew strong.

Historian Sima Tan, father of Sima Qian, later sorted the thinkers into six schools, including Confucians, Daoists, Mohists and Legalists. Scholars today note these labels were made after the fact. Many thinkers borrowed from more than one.

words.d: followers of Mozi, who taught impartial care for all and opposed aggressive war
impartial care or universal love; Mozi's teaching to care for all people equally
thinkers such as Han Feizi who taught strict law, reward and punishment

look.title: Rough Dates of Key Thinkers
look.cite: Common scholarly estimates; exact dates are uncertain
look.prompt: Which thinkers lived closest in time? Who could have heard of Confucius's teachings already written down?

check.q: What did Mozi teach?
choices: Impartial care for all and opposition to aggressive war
check.why: Mozi taught jian ai, care for all, and opposed attacking wars.

check.q: What did Legalists believe drove people?
check.why: Legalists like Han Feizi held that people respond mainly to reward and punishment.

check.q: Who sorted early thinkers into six schools?
check.why: Sima Tan, father of Sima Qian, named six schools; scholars note the labels came later.

lessons.title: Reading an Old Debate
lessons.mainIdea: The schools answered each other, so each one is easier to understand beside its rivals.
reading: The Hundred Schools did not think alone. Mencius, a Confucian, attacked Mozi's teaching of equal love, saying it ignored special duties to one's own father. Han Feizi, a Legalist, mocked Confucians for praising ancient kings in a changed world.

Mencius also met rulers who wanted quick gains. In Mencius 1A.1, King Hui of Liang asks how Mencius can *profit* his kingdom. Mencius replies that he brings only humaneness and rightness; if everyone seeks profit, the kingdom will be in danger.

Reading these *debates* helps you see what each school cared about most. A Confucian stressed family and virtue. A Mohist stressed fairness to all. A Legalist stressed order and power. A Daoist questioned all of their busy plans.

words.d: an argument in which people give reasons for different views
gain or advantage; Mencius criticized rulers who put profit first

look.title: Why Speak of Profit?
look.text: King Hui asks Mencius what he has brought to profit the kingdom. Mencius asks why the king must speak of profit. He says he brings only humaneness and rightness, and warns that if ruler and people all seek profit, the state will be in danger.
look.cite: Mencius 1A.1, paraphrased from James Legge, The Works of Mencius, The Chinese Classics vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1895)
look.prompt: What does Mencius think will happen if everyone seeks profit? How might a Legalist answer him?

check.q: What did Mencius criticize about Mozi's teaching?
choices: It was too strict about law
It ignored special duties to one's own family
check.why: Mencius said Mozi's equal love ignored the special bond with one's own father.

check.q: In Mencius 1A.1, what does King Hui want?
check.why: King Hui asks how Mencius can profit his kingdom; Mencius answers with humaneness and rightness.

check.q: Which school questioned all the others' busy plans?
check.why: Daoist texts question ambitious plans and praise acting without forcing.
